presentation: HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:,  Ms. Connor is a 50-year-old female who returns to clinic for a wound check.  The patient underwent an APR secondary to refractory ulcerative colitis.  Subsequently, she developed a wound infection, which has since healed.  On our most recent visit to our clinic, she has her perineal stitches removed and presents today for followup of her perineal wound.  She describes no drainage or erythema from her bottom.  She is having good ostomy output.  She does not describe any fevers, chills, nausea, or vomiting.  The patient does describe some intermittent pain beneath the upper portion of the incision as well as in the right lower quadrant below her ostomy.  She has been taking Percocet for this pain and it does work.  She has since run out has been trying extra strength Tylenol, which will occasionally help this intermittent pain.  She is requesting additional pain medications for this occasional abdominal pain, which she still experiences.,PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: , Temperature 95.8, pulse 68, blood pressure 132/73, and weight 159 pounds.  This is a pleasant female in no acute distress.  The patient's abdomen is soft, nontender, nondistended with a well-healed midline scar.  There is an ileostomy in the right hemiabdomen, which is pink, patent, productive, and protuberant.  There are no signs of masses or hernias over the patient's abdomen.,
human_ap: ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: , This is a pleasant 50-year-old female who has undergone an APR secondary to refractory ulcerative colitis.  Overall, her quality of life has significantly improved since she had her APR.  She is functioning well with her ileostomy.  She did have concerns or questions about her diet and we discussed the BRAT diet, which consisted of foods that would slow down the digestive tract such as bananas, rice, toast, cheese, and peanut butter.  I discussed the need to monitor her ileostomy output and preferential amount of daily output is 2 liters or less.  I have counseled her on refraining from soft drinks and fruit drinks.  I have also discussed with her that this diet is moreover a trial and error and that she may try certain foods that did not agree with her ileostomy, however others may and that this is something she will just have to perform trials with over the next several months until she finds what foods that she can and cannot eat with her ileostomy.  She also had questions about her occasional abdominal pain.  I told her that this was probably continue to improve as months went by and I gave her a refill of her Percocet for the continued occasional pain.  I told her that this would the last time I would refill the Percocet and if she has continued pain after she finishes this bottle then she would need to start ibuprofen or Tylenol if she had continued pain.  The patient then brought up some right hand and arm numbness, which has been there postsurgically and was thought to be from positioning during surgery.  This is all primarily gone away except for a little bit of numbness at the tip of the third digit as well as some occasional forearm muscle cramping.  I told her that I felt that this would continue to improve as it has done over the past two months since her surgery.  I told her to continue doing hand exercises as she has been doing and this seems to be working for her.  Overall, I think she has healed from her surgery and is doing very well.  Again, her quality of life is significantly improved.  She is happy with her performance.  We will see her back in six months just for a general routine checkup and see how she is doing at that time.
human_diagnoses: Post-operative status following abdominoperineal resection (APR) for refractory ulcerative colitis
Right hand and arm numbness and forearm muscle cramping, likely postsurgical neuropathy
human_dx_summary: A 50-year-old female is recovering well post-APR for refractory ulcerative colitis with improved quality of life, managing her ileostomy and occasional abdominal pain, and experiencing resolving postsurgical right hand and arm numbness.
llm_plan:
1. ASSESSMENT:
- Post-operative incisional/neuropathic pain: most likely given timing after APR, intermittent nature localized to scar/RLQ, absence of systemic or peritoneal signs, and partial relief with acetaminophen.
- Adhesions causing intermittent bowel tethering: plausible after major abdominal surgery, consistent with episodic pain and normal ostomy output without obstructive symptoms.
- Parastomal or incisional hernia (reducible): common late complication of stoma surgery; pain occurs without current exam findings of bulge or incarceration.

Can't-miss diagnoses: occult intra-abdominal abscess or early bowel obstruction (could progress to sepsis/perforation); strangulated hernia.

2. PLAN:
- For post-operative pain: continue non-opioid analgesia with scheduled acetaminophen 1 g TID PRN; avoid new opioid prescription given healing phase and abuse risk. Counsel on activity modification and warm compresses.
- For adhesions: no imaging needed now; advance diet as tolerated and monitor output.
- For hernia: reinforce abdominal-wall precautions; no ultrasound unless bulge or acute pain develops.
- To exclude abscess/obstruction/strangulated hernia: return precautions for fever, vomiting, obstipation, or increasing pain; urgent surgical re-evaluation if these occur. Otherwise, routine 4-week clinic follow-up for ostomy and wound surveillance. No labs or imaging at this visit.
llm_dx_summary: The patient is experiencing post-operative incisional/neuropathic pain likely related to recent APR surgery, with possible adhesions causing intermittent bowel tethering and a reducible parastomal or incisional hernia without current complications.

llm_plan:
1. ASSESSMENT:
- Paclitaxel-induced peripheral neuropathy: unilateral upper-extremity paresthesias began immediately after completing six cycles of carboplatin/paclitaxel; taxanes are the most common cause of dose-dependent sensory neuropathy in this setting and symptoms have remained stable.
- Stage 1 hypertension (white-coat component possible): office BP 143/83 in a patient already voicing concern; no end-organ symptoms.
- Benign cutaneous nevus: stable pigmented lesion on scalp noticed for months by the patient; no change, bleeding, or irregular features described.

Can't-miss diagnoses: brain metastasis or cerebrovascular event (stroke/TIA) causing focal sensory symptoms; ovarian-cancer recurrence with occult peritoneal or nodal disease despite recent CT.

2. PLAN:
- Neuropathy: no laboratory or electrodiagnostic testing indicated at this time because symptoms are mild, non-progressive, and lack motor deficit; counsel on safety (falls, burns) and schedule telephone follow-up in 4 weeks to confirm stability.
- Hypertension: instruct patient to record home BP twice weekly for 2 weeks using existing cuff; review log at next visit; no new medication or laboratory panel today.
- Mole: perform focused scalp examination today; if features remain reassuring (symmetric, uniform color, <6 mm), photograph and re-inspect in 3 months; no dermatology referral.
- Exclude brain metastasis/cerebrovascular event: obtain non-contrast head CT only if new headache, vomiting, or focal weakness develops; otherwise defer given normal neurologic exam and recent negative body CT.
- Exclude recurrence: continue scheduled surveillance CT abdomen/pelvis in 3–6 months per oncology protocol; no additional imaging or tumor markers today.
- Follow-up: return in 4–6 weeks with home BP log and interval symptom review; sooner if neurologic symptoms worsen.

Final answer: 1. ASSESSMENT: Paclitaxel-induced peripheral neuropathy (timing post-taxane, stable sensory sx); stage 1 HTN (BP 143/83); benign scalp nevus (patient concern, no red flags). Can't-miss: brain met/CVA; occult recurrence. 2. PLAN: observe neuropathy, home BP log, inspect mole; head CT only if neuro worsening; routine surveillance CT later; f/u 4-6 wk.
llm_dx_summary: The patient presents with stable unilateral upper-extremity sensory neuropathy likely induced by paclitaxel, accompanied by stage 1 hypertension and a benign scalp nevus.

llm_plan:
1. ASSESSMENT:
- Large local reaction to hymenoptera (wasp) sting: most likely; matches timing (onset <24 h), history of identical prior episodes limited to swelling at sting site, and exam showing non-tender, non-erythematous edema without systemic features.
- Early cellulitis: possible but less probable; sting provides portal, yet absence of pain, warmth, or erythema lowers likelihood.
- Type-IV delayed hypersensitivity: plausible given localized progression without IgE-mediated signs.

Can't-miss diagnoses: anaphylaxis (airway/cardiovascular compromise); compartment syndrome (forearm swelling compromising perfusion).

2. PLAN:
- Large local reaction: elevate arm, apply ice 15 min qid, OTC cetirizine 10 mg daily + ibuprofen 400 mg q6h PRN; no labs/imaging. Return immediately for dyspnea, throat tightness, or rapid swelling spread.
- Cellulitis: no antibiotics; re-examine in 48 h (or sooner if fever/pain develops) to assess for spreading erythema—only then would antibiotics be warranted.
- Hypersensitivity: same supportive measures; no testing required.

Exclude anaphylaxis: history and vitals already negative; educate on epinephrine auto-injector prescription only if future systemic symptoms occur (not indicated now).  
Exclude compartment syndrome: check capillary refill and pain on passive stretch today (normal); advise urgent return if disproportionate pain or numbness develops.  
No routine labs, cultures, or specialist referral; follow-up in 2–3 days or PRN worsening.
llm_diagnoses: Large local reaction to hymenoptera (wasp) sting
llm_dx_summary: The patient most likely has a large local reaction to a wasp sting characterized by localized non-tender edema without systemic symptoms, with early cellulitis and delayed hypersensitivity considered less probable.

Check capillary refill and pain on passive stretch today

llm_plan:
1. ASSESSMENT:
- Viral upper respiratory infection (URI) with post-nasal drip: acute sore throat, hoarse voice, low-grade fever, fatigue, posterior pharyngeal drainage, and negative rapid strep/culture plus normal Water’s view make this the most probable etiology.
- Allergic rhinitis (acute exacerbation): sudden-onset congestion, puffy eyelids, nasal mucosal edema/erythema, and partial response to diphenhydramine favor an allergic component, especially given the absence of bacterial findings.
- Early nephrotic syndrome (possible minimal-change disease): new periorbital edema, 14-lb weight gain, and prior hypertension raise concern for hypoalbuminemic edema; a recent URI can be a trigger.

Can't-miss diagnoses: acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (even with negative pharyngeal testing); periorbital/orbital cellulitis; retropharyngeal abscess.

2. PLAN:
- Viral URI/allergic rhinitis: supportive care only (continue OTC antihistamine PRN, saline nasal rinses, rest, hydration); no antibiotics or imaging indicated.
- Suspected nephrotic syndrome: obtain urine dipstick for protein (office-based, immediate result) and first-morning urine protein/creatinine ratio if dipstick ≥1+; check blood pressure today and schedule nurse-visit BP check in 48 h; counsel on low-salt diet and daily weights; refer to pediatric nephrology only if proteinuria confirmed or BP remains elevated.
- Exclude can't-miss diagnoses: repeat BP measurement and targeted eye exam today to rule out cellulitis (no proptosis, vision change, or fever >38.5 °C); neck remains supple without trismus or drooling, so no imaging for retropharyngeal abscess needed; urine dipstick also screens for glomerulonephritis. Return precautions given for worsening edema, dyspnea, or severe headache. Follow-up in 5–7 days or sooner if symptoms persist.

Final answer: 1. ASSESSMENT: Viral URI w/ post-nasal drip (acute sx + neg strep/imaging); allergic rhinitis (sudden congestion, puffy lids, nasal edema); early nephrotic synd (periorbital edema + wt gain + prior HTN). Can't-miss: PSGN, periorbital cellulitis, retropharyngeal abscess. 2. PLAN: supportive care only for URI/rhinitis; urine dipstick + prot/Cr ratio + serial BP for nephrotic/AGN; no routine labs/imaging; f/u 5-7d or sooner if worsening.
llm_diagnoses: Viral upper respiratory infection (URI) with post-nasal drip
llm_dx_summary: The patient most likely has a viral upper respiratory infection with post-nasal drip, complicated by allergic rhinitis and early signs of nephrotic syndrome.

llm_plan:
1. ASSESSMENT:
- Seasonal allergic rhinitis: Classic symptoms (itchy/watery eyes, rhinorrhea, sneezing, ear pressure) with matching exam findings of clear nasal discharge and watery ocular drainage in a patient with known seasonal pattern.
- External hemorrhoids (postpartum): Focal bright-red rectal bleeding and pain with defecation plus visible inflamed external hemorrhoid on anoscopy; common after vaginal delivery due to straining and venous congestion.
- Normal postpartum recovery (involution + lochia): Uterus appropriately involuting, lochia progressing from red to brown/yellow, minimal volume, no cramping or fever at 3 weeks.

Can't-miss diagnoses: Postpartum endometritis or pelvic infection (fever, foul discharge, or uterine tenderness could indicate retained products or ascending infection); anal fissure or occult internal hemorrhoid/fistula (if bleeding persists despite treatment).

2. PLAN:
- Allergic rhinitis: Initiate non-sedating second-generation antihistamine (loratadine or cetirizine) or intranasal corticosteroid spray; avoid diphenhydramine given reported allergy. No labs or imaging needed.
- Hemorrhoids: Recommend sitz baths 2–3 times daily, fiber supplement (psyllium) or stool softener, and topical witch-hazel or hydrocortisone cream for 7 days. Return sooner if bleeding increases, pain worsens, or fever develops.
- Normal postpartum state: Continue prenatal vitamins and breastfeeding support; no contraception discussion yet as intercourse has not resumed. Counsel on warning signs (heavy bleeding, fever, severe pain).
- To exclude can't-miss: History and vital signs already reassuring (afebrile, normal BP, non-tender uterus); repeat pelvic exam and inquire about fever/discharge only if symptoms arise at follow-up. No routine cultures, CBC, or colonoscopy indicated at this visit given low-risk bleeding and identified external lesion. Follow-up in 6 weeks or sooner if symptoms persist.
llm_dx_summary: The patient presents with classic seasonal allergic rhinitis symptoms, postpartum external hemorrhoids causing rectal bleeding and pain, and is otherwise experiencing normal postpartum recovery without signs of infection.

llm_plan:
1. ASSESSMENT:
- Musculoskeletal/growing pains (most likely): bilateral lateral leg pain worse at night, fully responsive to simple analgesics, stable exam without new weakness, bowel/bladder change, or reflex abnormalities in an otherwise healthy adolescent.
- Retethered cord (symptomatic): prior lipomyomeningocele repairs, chronic L4–S1 sensory loss, and new nocturnal leg pain; classic timing for late retethering after growth spurt.
- Chronic neuropathic pain from residual sensory-root scarring: fixed patchy sensory loss since childhood, no progressive motor or sphincter findings.

Can't-miss diagnoses: progressive spinal-cord ischemia from tethering (risk of permanent paraparesis or incontinence); spinal infection (discitis/osteomyelitis); intraspinal tumor (rare but catastrophic if missed).

2. PLAN:
- Musculoskeletal/growing pains: continue scheduled NSAIDs + acetaminophen at bedtime; add nightly calf stretching; no imaging or labs.
- Retethered cord: counsel family on red-flag symptoms (new weakness, incontinence, gait change); schedule neurosurgery clinic follow-up in 3 months or sooner if symptoms worsen; MRI spine only if deficits progress (resource-limited setting, stable exam does not yet alter management).
- Neuropathic pain: same conservative regimen; no additional neuropathic agents unless pain disrupts sleep despite above measures.

To exclude can't-miss diagnoses: urgent MRI (with neurosurgical review) if any new motor deficit, hyperreflexia, or sphincter change appears; temperature and ESR/CRP only if fever or focal spinal tenderness develops (not present now). No routine labs, EMG, or broad imaging. Follow-up visit in 6–8 weeks to reassess symptoms and neurologic function.
llm_diagnoses: Chronic neuropathic pain from residual sensory-root scarring
llm_dx_summary: An otherwise healthy adolescent presents with bilateral lateral leg pain most likely due to musculoskeletal/growing pains, complicated by symptomatic retethered cord and chronic neuropathic pain from residual sensory-root scarring.

No bleeding problems have been noted.  I have spoken with her hematologist who recommends at this point we decrease her prednisone to 40 mg for 3 days and then go down to 20 mg a day. llm_plan:
1. ASSESSMENT:
- Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) responding to corticosteroids: established diagnosis with clear platelet rise (10 → 43) and resolution of petechiae after prednisone increase, consistent with typical steroid-responsive ITP.
- Steroid-dependent ITP: prior maintenance on low-dose alternate-day prednisone with platelets hovering just above 20 suggests ongoing requirement for therapy to prevent relapse.
- Possible secondary ITP (e.g., mild autoimmune or post-viral trigger): no new systemic features but remains plausible in adults without exhaustive exclusion of underlying causes.

Can't-miss diagnoses: intracranial or mucosal hemorrhage (platelets <10–20 with bleeding); bone-marrow failure or leukemia (new severe thrombocytopenia unresponsive to steroids); TTP/HUS (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia).

2. PLAN:
- Taper prednisone exactly as recommended by hematology (40 mg daily × 3 days → 20 mg daily) to minimize cumulative steroid exposure while maintaining response.
- Check CBC with platelet count in 7–10 days (or sooner if bleeding occurs) to confirm stability on the lower dose; no other blood work or imaging indicated at this time.
- Counsel patient on bleeding precautions and prompt return for petechiae, epistaxis, or neurologic symptoms; continue current follow-up interval with hematology.
- No bone-marrow biopsy, autoantibody panel, or additional referrals needed unless platelets fall again or new cytopenias appear.

(The plan uses only actions that directly guide the steroid taper and detect clinically important relapse or bleeding.)
llm_diagnoses: Possible secondary ITP (e.g., mild autoimmune or post-viral trigger)
llm_dx_summary: The patient has steroid-responsive immune thrombocytopenia with a recent platelet count improvement, requiring ongoing low-dose prednisone to prevent relapse.

1. ASSESSMENT:
- Plantar fasciitis: classic post-static dyskinesia (first-step morning pain) worsening with activity, focal tenderness at medial calcaneal tubercle with radiation along medial arch, no systemic features.
- Heel-pad atrophy or contusion: mechanical heel pain with activity; possible in active patients but lacks the prominent morning stiffness seen here.
- Tarsal-tunnel syndrome (entrapment of posterior tibial nerve): medial heel/arch pain that may worsen with prolonged standing/walking; less likely without paresthesias or positive Tinel sign.

Can't-miss diagnoses: calcaneal stress fracture (risk of completion fracture if weight-bearing continues); calcaneal osteomyelitis (rapid tissue destruction if missed, though afebrile with intact skin).

2. PLAN:
- Plantar fasciitis: begin home plantar-fascia and Achilles stretching 3–4 times daily, OTC NSAIDs PRN with food if no contraindications, advise supportive shoes with soft heel cushion or over-the-counter orthotic insert; return in 4 weeks or sooner if pain escalates.
- Heel-pad atrophy/contusion and tarsal-tunnel syndrome: same initial conservative measures above; no additional testing needed at this visit.
- Exclude calcaneal stress fracture: counsel strict activity modification (avoid running/jumping, use cane if limp present) and return immediately for plain-film radiograph if pain becomes constant at rest or night pain develops.
- Exclude osteomyelitis: no imaging or labs indicated now given intact skin, absence of fever/chills, and short symptom duration; educate on warning signs (redness, swelling, fever) and urgent return if they appear.
- No routine labs, advanced imaging, or specialist referral at this initial visit. Follow-up in 4 weeks to reassess response.

- Mild chronic GVHD (GI/skin/liver) stable off immunosuppression: 53 months post-allogeneic transplant with only mild ongoing symptoms and no therapy required.
- Multifactorial anemia (Hb 10.1) with possible occult GI blood loss: history of hematochezia, recent benign endoscopy with polypectomy, mild thrombocytopenia, and chronic disease.
- Fatigue related to anemia, obesity, and polypharmacy (psychotropics, sedatives): matches reported symptoms and activity limitation without new focal findings.

Can't-miss diagnoses: Mantle-cell lymphoma relapse (prior autologous failure, now 4.5 years post-allogeneic); colorectal malignancy or significant ongoing GI bleed (prior hematochezia despite benign endoscopy).

2. PLAN:
- Continue current GVHD surveillance with q4-8 week visits and CBC/LFTs only; no immunosuppression restart unless symptoms worsen.
- For anemia/fatigue: obtain iron studies, B12/folate, and fecal occult blood x3 only if not recently performed; otherwise continue supportive care (current Lasix, potassium, Nexium) and monitor Hb trend.
- To exclude relapse: peripheral blood flow cytometry for minimal residual disease at next visit; proceed to marrow biopsy only if counts drop further or circulating abnormal cells appear.
- To exclude colorectal malignancy: repeat colonoscopy in 3 years per post-polypectomy guidelines or sooner only if bleeding recurs or iron deficiency worsens; no immediate imaging or specialist re-referral.
- Medication review: consolidate Paxil/Prozac to single SSRI to reduce polypharmacy burden; continue all other agents unchanged.
- Follow-up in 6 weeks with interval CBC and symptom check; return sooner for new bleeding, fever, or weight loss.

Final answer: see structured ASSESSMENT/PLAN above.

llm_plan:
1. ASSESSMENT:
- Delirium superimposed on dementia (most likely): fluctuating confusion, disorientation to season, and one episode of inappropriate defecation in a patient already on donepezil; common in nursing-home residents and often multifactorial.
- Polypharmacy/medication adverse effects: chronic use of alprazolam, digoxin, beta-blocker, and PRN agents readily explains listlessness, weakness, and intermittent mental-status changes.
- Late-life depression/apathy syndrome: progressive weight loss, anorexia, and amotivation despite stable vital signs and non-focal exam.

Can't-miss diagnoses: urinary-tract infection (occult source of delirium), digoxin toxicity or electrolyte imbalance (arrhythmia risk), subdural hematoma (remote fall history plus anticoagulation).

2. PLAN:
- Obtain urine dipstick or limited urinalysis only if dipstick leukocyte/nitrite positive; treat empirically with nitrofurantoin 100 mg BID × 3 days if positive and no sulfa allergy.
- Review medication list today: discontinue alprazolam and PRN furosemide; check finger-stick or serum digoxin level only if pulse <50 or new arrhythmia; hold next digoxin dose if level >1.5 ng/mL.
- Trial of oral nutritional supplement (Ensure 1 can TID) as requested; weigh weekly; screen for depression with single question (“Do you feel down?”) at next visit—no labs or imaging unless weight loss accelerates >5 %.
- Fall precautions and PT for gait already in place; no head CT unless new focal deficit or coagulopathy develops.
- Return in 1 week or sooner if confusion worsens, fever, or vomiting; family/nursing staff to report any change in mental status immediately.

Final answer: 1. Delirium on dementia (multifactorial); 2. Polypharmacy effects; 3. Depression. Can't-miss: UTI, digoxin toxicity/electrolytes, subdural. Plan: UA only if dipstick +, deprescribe alprazolam/digoxin check if indicated, Ensure trial, weekly weights, 1-wk f/u.
llm_dx_summary: An elderly nursing-home resident presents with multifactorial delirium superimposed on dementia, likely exacerbated by polypharmacy and late-life depression.

1. ASSESSMENT:
- Esophageal dysmotility (tertiary contractions with delayed emptying): explains odynophagia/dysphagia; directly corroborated by recent barium swallow.
- Post-thrombotic syndrome/chronic venous insufficiency: accounts for progressive unilateral calf enlargement in patient with two prior DVTs; no acute tenderness or exam edema lowers acuity but does not exclude chronic sequelae.
- Benign simple renal cyst (enlarging): typical imaging appearance; most such cysts remain indolent and asymptomatic.

Can't-miss diagnoses:
- Recurrent or new lung cancer (post-lobectomy NSCLC surveillance).
- Acute or propagating lower-extremity DVT (prior DVT history + unilateral calf change).

2. PLAN:
- Esophageal dysmotility: trial of twice-daily PPI for 4 weeks plus head-of-bed elevation and small frequent meals; return sooner if weight loss or progressive symptoms; no endoscopy or manometry unless failure of conservative measures.
- Post-thrombotic changes: venous duplex ultrasound of left leg (one-time, indicated by history plus size change) to exclude acute DVT; continue aspirin 81 mg daily; no stockings or anticoagulation unless clot confirmed.
- Renal cyst: no immediate imaging or urology referral; document size on existing CT and repeat limited renal ultrasound only in 6–12 months if patient develops flank pain or hematuria.
- Cancer surveillance: continue annual low-dose chest radiograph (already obtained and negative); no CT or specialist referral while asymptomatic with normal exam and radiograph.
- Follow-up visit in 6 months or sooner for new/worsening symptoms; medication reconciliation reviewed.

Final answer: 1. ASSESSMENT: Esophageal dysmotility (tertiary contractions); post-thrombotic calf changes; benign renal cyst. Can't-miss: recurrent lung ca, acute DVT. 2. PLAN: PPI trial + lifestyle for dysphagia; duplex US for calf; no renal f/u now; annual CXR surveillance; 6-mo return.

llm_plan:
1. ASSESSMENT:
- Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure due to cardiogenic pulmonary edema: most probable given new/increased bibasilar crackles in an intubated patient; fluid overload or left-ventricular dysfunction produces dependent crackles and impairs gas exchange.
- Hospital-acquired or aspiration pneumonia: common in recently intubated patients; crackles reflect focal consolidation and impaired clearance while sedated.
- Atelectasis with mucus plugging: frequent in the first 24–48 h of mechanical ventilation; dependent crackles arise from alveolar collapse without infection or heart failure.

Can't-miss diagnoses: tension pneumothorax (rapid decompensation on positive-pressure ventilation); pulmonary embolism (sudden increase in dead-space and hypoxia).

2. PLAN:
- Cardiogenic edema: obtain ECG and bedside cardiac ultrasound (if available) to evaluate for wall-motion abnormality or reduced EF; if present, initiate diuresis with furosemide 20–40 mg IV and restrict fluids; daily weights and strict I/O.
- Pneumonia: send endotracheal aspirate for Gram stain/culture before any antibiotics; start empiric vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam only if aspirate shows organisms or new fever/leukocytosis develops.
- Atelectasis: perform recruitment maneuver and increase PEEP by 2–3 cm H₂O; scheduled suctioning and chest physiotherapy; reassess crackles and PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio in 4–6 h.
- Exclude tension pneumothorax: immediate bilateral chest auscultation and percussion; if unilateral absent breath sounds or hypotension, perform needle decompression followed by tube thoracostomy.
- Exclude PE: if sudden rise in PaCO₂–ETCO₂ gradient or unexplained tachycardia/hypotension occurs, obtain lower-extremity Doppler ultrasound (resource-appropriate first step) before considering CT pulmonary angiography.
- Supportive care: continue current ventilator settings with daily sedation vacation and spontaneous breathing trial; head-of-bed elevation 30–45°; DVT prophylaxis with unfractionated heparin 5000 U SQ q8h; reassess extubation readiness each morning. No routine labs or daily CXR unless clinical change.

Follow-up: re-evaluate in 6–12 h or sooner if hemodynamics or oxygenation deteriorate.

1. ASSESSMENT:
- Statin-associated muscle symptoms (myalgia): Temporal onset with high-dose Lipitor, bilateral leg pain without focal neuro deficits or exertional claudication; statin discontinued today.
- Lumbar radiculopathy (L5–S1): Pain radiating from buttocks to leg/ankle, positional, with preserved reflexes and negative straight-leg raise on exam.

Can't-miss diagnoses: Spinal infection/malignancy (night sweats, fever, unintentional weight loss, age >50); critical spinal stenosis with impending cauda equina.

2. PLAN:
- Statin myalgia: No further labs or imaging needed now that Lipitor stopped; switch to pravastatin 20 mg daily if LDL goal unmet at next visit; recheck symptoms and CK only if pain persists/worsens.
- Radiculopathy: Conservative care—acetaminophen 500 mg TID PRN, encourage continued water aerobics, limit heavy lifting; MRI lumbar spine only if progressive weakness, bowel/bladder changes, or no improvement in 6 weeks.

- Diabetes: Continue reduced Glucovance 1.25/250 daily; fasting glucose log review at 1-month return; no new A1c or panels today.
- Follow-up: Return in 4 weeks or sooner for worsening pain, fever, or neuro changes; reinforce diet and exercise.

Final answer: ASSESSMENT: 1. Statin myalgia (temporal link to Lipitor). 2. Lumbar radiculopathy (buttock-to-leg radiation). 3. Nocturnal cramps (DM, nighttime pattern). Can't-miss: spinal infection/malignancy (B symptoms + age). PLAN: Stop statin already done; acetaminophen PRN + activity mod; CBC/ESR to r/o can't-miss; 4-wk f/u; no routine imaging/labs.

1. ASSESSMENT:
- IgE-mediated food allergy to carrot/celery (Apiaceae family): immediate reproducible vomiting/pain 5–10 min after ingestion of the implicated raw vegetables is the classic temporal pattern for type-I hypersensitivity.
- Oral allergy syndrome (pollen–food cross-reactivity): same foods commonly provoke symptoms in pollen-sensitized children; systemic signs are absent and cooked forms are usually tolerated.
- Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (behavioral): emerging picky eating can amplify or mimic mild adverse reactions, yet the stereotyped, food-specific timing favors an organic trigger.

Can't-miss diagnoses: evolving anaphylaxis or biphasic reaction (airway/cardiovascular compromise after repeat exposure); eosinophilic esophagitis or other eosinophilic GI disorder (progressive dysphagia/failure to thrive).

- Food allergy/OAS: strict avoidance of raw carrot and celery; provide written emergency plan and educate caregivers on recognition of escalating symptoms (hives, wheezing, hypotension). No skin-prick testing or serum IgE panels at this visit—result would not alter initial management of avoidance. If future exposures provoke respiratory or cardiovascular signs, refer to nearest allergy service for epinephrine auto-injector prescription and supervised challenge.
- Behavioral component: continue ad-lib normal diet excluding the two triggers; weigh at each well-child visit to confirm ongoing weight gain. No growth labs or swallow study indicated while weight trajectory remains normal.
- Can't-miss exclusion: no routine endoscopy or pH probe; instead, schedule nurse phone follow-up in 2 weeks and prompt in-person visit if vomiting spreads to other foods, weight stalls, or respiratory symptoms appear. No medications, imaging, or specialist referral required at present.

Follow-up: routine well-child visit in 3 months or sooner if symptoms change.

1. ASSESSMENT:
- Iatrogenic nasal septal perforation (most likely): clear temporal association with prior septoplasty; anterior location and well-healed edges on exam match typical surgical complication; explains ongoing dryness, “stretching” pressure, and epistaxis via loss of normal humidification and turbulent airflow.
- Secondary rhinitis sicca / mucosal drying: direct consequence of the perforation; produces the patient’s reported dryness and intermittent bleeding despite saline washes; no crusting seen today but symptoms persist.
- Minor local irritation or low-grade vestibulitis: accounts for residual discomfort; exam shows no active infection or crusting, making this a diagnosis of exclusion after the above.

Can't-miss diagnoses: granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) or other systemic vasculitis; chronic cocaine insufflation; occult intranasal malignancy or chronic invasive infection. These can produce or enlarge septal perforations and must be excluded by history and, if red flags present, targeted testing.

2. PLAN:
- Continue and optimize topical care for perforation-related dryness: increase saline rinses to 3–4 times daily; add over-the-counter nasal saline gel or a thin film of petroleum jelly to the perforation edges twice daily to restore moisture and reduce epistaxis. No antibiotics or steroids needed absent infection or inflammation.
- Behavioral measures: counsel against digital trauma, forceful nose-blowing, or irritants; advise cool-mist humidifier at night.
- Exclude can't-miss diagnoses: obtain focused history for sinonasal cocaine use, chronic sinusitis, arthralgias, hemoptysis, or weight loss. If any positive responses or atypical features (posterior perforation, active crusting/granulation, systemic symptoms) emerge, send ANCA serology and refer to ENT for biopsy; otherwise, no serologic or imaging work-up required.
- Follow-up: return in 4–6 weeks or sooner if epistaxis increases, pain worsens, or new systemic symptoms develop. No routine labs, cultures, or imaging at this visit.

No referrals or advanced testing indicated given clear post-surgical etiology and limited resources.

1. ASSESSMENT:
- Localized (non-IgE-mediated) reaction to hymenoptera venom: acute, strictly unilateral hand erythema/edema at sting sites, no systemic features, and prior sting tolerated; classic time course.
- Early cellulitis/superinfection: possible bacterial entry via sting puncture, though timing (<12 h) makes this less probable than sterile inflammation.
- Large local reaction (type-IV hypersensitivity): can expand over 24–48 h to >10 cm; still confined to skin/subcutis without airway or vital-sign changes.

Can't-miss diagnoses: anaphylaxis/impending airway compromise; necrotizing soft-tissue infection.

2. PLAN:
- Localized reaction: continue non-sedating antihistamine (loratadine 10 mg daily PRN × 3–5 d); cool compresses, elevate hand, remove constrictive jewelry (already done); return immediately for dyspnea, diffuse rash, or swelling beyond wrist.
- Cellulitis: no antibiotics yet; mark borders with pen and re-evaluate in 24 h (or sooner if fever/redness spreads rapidly); only if progression occurs, start empiric oral cephalexin (resource-appropriate, non-sulfa).
- Large local reaction: same supportive measures; if swelling crosses wrist or impairs function at follow-up, short-course oral prednisone 40 mg × 3 d (no taper needed).

Exclude can't-miss diagnoses: history and exam already exclude anaphylaxis (normal vitals, patent airway, no urticaria/bronchospasm); educate on return precautions for epinephrine auto-injector prescription only if systemic symptoms recur. No imaging/labs indicated; necrotizing infection excluded by lack of pain out of proportion, crepitus, or systemic toxicity—recheck in 24 h or sooner if systemic signs develop. No routine bloodwork, ECG, or referral required. Follow-up with primary care in 48 h or ED if worsening.
llm_dx_summary: The patient presents with a localized non-IgE-mediated reaction to a hymenoptera sting characterized by acute unilateral hand erythema and edema without systemic involvement, with possible early cellulitis and large local type-IV hypersensitivity reaction considered.

1. ASSESSMENT:
- Bronchopulmonary dysplasia with chronic ventilator dependence: history of 22-week prematurity, current 2.5 L O2 requirement, and progressive sprint tolerance to 4.5 h twice daily with only mild tachypnea and wheezing on exam.
- G-tube dependence with enteral feeding intolerance: recurrent abdominal distension and constipation triggered by Pediasure, now improved on Isomil 24 cal plus purees; recent Mic-key upsizing and silver-nitrate therapy.
- Mild constipation secondary to formula: directly linked to dietary changes and responsive to Colace and fiber adjustment.

Can't-miss diagnoses: acute respiratory decompensation or ventilator-associated pneumonia; G-tube site cellulitis, abscess, or buried bumper; bowel obstruction or severe fecal impaction.

2. PLAN:
- Continue current sprint schedule and 2.5 L O2; increase sprint duration by 15 min every 3 days only if RR remains <50 and no increased work of breathing; return immediately for fever, increased O2 need, or lethargy.
- Maintain Isomil 24 cal + pureed feeds at current volume; hold Pediasure; titrate Colace to one soft stool daily; weigh weekly and report loss >4 oz.
- Continue silver nitrate to G-tube site three times weekly; keep site dry; foster mother to photograph any erythema or drainage and call.
- To exclude acute respiratory infection: obtain pulse-oximetry spot check and respiratory-rate trend only if new fever or O2 desaturation occurs (no routine CXR or CBC).
- To exclude G-tube complication: visual inspection of site at every visit; immediate referral to Dr. XYZ for any skin breakdown or feeding difficulty.
- To exclude obstruction: abdominal exam at each visit; urgent surgical evaluation only if vomiting, absent bowel sounds, or marked distension recurs.
- Foster-care respite admission arranged for 19–23rd; coordinate with social work for ventilator-capable facility; follow-up with pulmonology, GI, and ophthalmology as scheduled; return in 4 weeks or sooner for weight or respiratory change.

llm_plan:
1. ASSESSMENT:
- Chronic nonallergic rhinitis (most likely): persistent nasal congestion/snorting with inferior turbinate edema after documented negative allergy testing and cessation of antihistamines; no nocturnal snoring reported.
- Mild paronychia/ingrown toenail, right hallux: focal lateral erythema and periungual dryness/peeling for 1.5 weeks in setting of very short nails (suggesting trauma or nail-biting).
- Xerosis/dermatitis of toe skin: dryness and peeling without drainage, fever, or spreading erythema.

Can't-miss diagnoses: (1) bacterial cellulitis or deeper soft-tissue infection of toe; (2) adenoidal hypertrophy causing chronic nasal obstruction (consider if symptoms persist).

2. PLAN:
- Nonallergic rhinitis: initiate daily nasal saline irrigation; add OTC intranasal corticosteroid spray (e.g., fluticasone) if no improvement in 2 weeks; counsel on trigger avoidance. No imaging or further allergy testing.
- Paronychia/ingrown toenail: warm soaks 2–3 times daily, keep area clean/dry, advise proper straight-across nail trimming; return promptly for fever, pus, or spreading redness.
- Xerosis: apply bland emollient (petrolatum) to toe BID.
- To exclude can't-miss cellulitis: instruct family to monitor for systemic signs and return in 48 h if worsening; no antibiotics or cultures unless progression occurs.
- To exclude adenoid hypertrophy: reassess nasal symptoms and sleep in 4 weeks; refer to ENT for nasopharyngoscopy only if persistent severe obstruction develops.
- Follow-up: return in 3–4 weeks or sooner if toe worsens; no labs, imaging, or specialist referrals at this visit.

Final answer: 1. ASSESSMENT: Chronic nonallergic rhinitis (persistent congestion + turbinate edema post-negative allergy testing); mild paronychia/ingrown toenail right hallux (lateral erythema, short nails); toe xerosis/dermatitis. Can't-miss: bacterial cellulitis; adenoid hypertrophy. 2. PLAN: saline ± nasal steroid spray; warm soaks + nail care; emollient; monitor for cellulitis progression; recheck nose in 4 wk (ENT only if severe). No routine tests/referrals.

1. ASSESSMENT:
- Viral upper respiratory infection with post-nasal drip: most common cause of subacute afebrile cough + congestion in toddlers; visible posterior pharyngeal drainage and shotty nodes support this.
- Post-viral cough (airway hyper-reactivity): cough often lingers 2–4 weeks after viral URI; normal lung exam and CXR fit.
- Mild bacterial sinusitis: purulent drainage, family exposure (sibling with sinusitis), duration >10 days.

Can't-miss: Aspirated foreign body (pop-can tab); occult pneumonia (despite normal CXR).

2. PLAN:
- Viral URI/post-nasal drip: nasal saline drops + bulb suction q4–6 h PRN; cool-mist humidifier; acetaminophen 15 mg/kg q6 h PRN fever/pain; return precautions (worsening cough, fever, respiratory distress).
- Post-viral cough: continue supportive care above; no cough suppressant or bronchodilator needed at this time.
- Bacterial sinusitis: watchful waiting (no antibiotics yet); re-evaluate in 48–72 h if fever or worsening symptoms develop.

Exclude can't-miss diagnoses: CXR already performed (no FB or infiltrate); continue close observation at home with mother instructed to return immediately for any respiratory distress, unilateral wheeze, or fever. No further imaging or specialist referral required unless symptoms progress.

Follow-up: office visit or phone call in 5–7 days; sooner if any red-flag symptoms. No routine labs or additional tests.

1. ASSESSMENT:
- Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (most likely): persistent thick purulent nasal drainage and post-nasal drip since April 14 without resolution, plus referred otalgia and swollen erythematous nares; duration exceeds typical viral illness.
- Viral upper respiratory infection with prominent post-nasal drip: ongoing congestion, loose cough, gray/distorted TMs without erythema, afebrile and non-toxic.
- Otitis media with effusion (bilateral): dull gray TMs with lost light reflexes but no bulging/erythema, consistent with eustachian-tube dysfunction from nasal inflammation.
- Can't-miss: mastoiditis or early orbital extension (periorbital puffiness); both require prompt exclusion given proximity to sinuses/ears.

2. PLAN:
- No routine labs, cultures, or imaging (low-yield in uncomplicated pediatric rhinosinusitis).
- Start amoxicillin-clavulanate 45 mg/kg/day divided BID × 10 days (covers resistant organisms after recent amoxicillin exposure).
- Supportive care only: saline nasal rinses or spray, acetaminophen or ibuprofen PRN pain, head elevation, humidified air; counsel on expected 7–10 day improvement.
- Strict return precautions today for fever, severe headache, vision change, facial swelling, or lethargy to exclude mastoiditis/orbital spread.
- Follow-up in 48–72 h by phone or visit; if no improvement, reconsider referral (scarce) for possible sinus imaging or ENT evaluation.

Final answer: 1. ASSESSMENT: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (persistent purulent drainage >10 days, referred otalgia); Viral URI w/ post-nasal drip (afebrile, non-toxic, gray TMs); OME 2/2 eustachian dysfunction. - Exclude PE: Wells score low-moderate; perform D-dimer; if positive, proceed to CT pulmonary angiogram only if result alters anticoagulation decision.
- Exclude ACS: given atypical symptoms and normal ECG, no troponin or urgent referral; advise immediate return if chest pain develops.
- Follow-up: return in 1 week or sooner if symptoms worsen; no other labs or referrals at this time.

llm_plan:
1. ASSESSMENT:
- Late-onset rheumatoid arthritis (or inflammatory polyarthritis): Most likely given symmetric doughy MCP/wrist involvement, NSAID nonresponse, and functional decline without alternative explanation.
- Primary generalized osteoarthritis: Common at age 77 with hand/wrist predominance; may coexist with or mimic inflammatory disease.
- Medication-related or multifactorial arthralgia (NSAID inefficacy plus possible contribution from depression/immobility): Supported by lack of objective synovitis beyond mild doughiness and recent functional worsening.

Can't-miss diagnoses: Septic arthritis/osteomyelitis (prior discitis history); giant-cell arteritis/polymyalgia rheumatica overlap; hypercalcemia-related arthropathy or occult myeloma (Ca 10.8, anemia, renal impairment).

2. PLAN:
- Inflammatory arthritis: Trial switch from Daypro to acetaminophen 1 g TID PRN (renal-sparing); obtain hand/wrist X-rays only if they will alter decision for DMARD referral. Check CRP if available and low-cost to support inflammation.
- Osteoarthritis: Continue conservative measures (activity as tolerated, acetaminophen); no imaging or specialist referral unless function deteriorates further.
- Stop Daypro immediately (elevated Cr/BUN); monitor renal function in 1–2 weeks if feasible. Resume Zoloft and address depression with supportive counseling.
- Exclude septic arthritis/osteomyelitis: History/exam alone (afebrile, no erythema) sufficient; no joint aspiration unless focal redness/swelling develops.
- Exclude GCA/PMR: Inquire specifically about new headache, jaw claudication, or scalp tenderness at follow-up; no ESR unless symptoms present.
- Exclude myeloma/hypercalcemia arthropathy: No serum protein electrophoresis; repeat calcium and CBC only if new constitutional symptoms or worsening anemia.
- Follow-up in 4–6 weeks for joint response, mobility, and BP/glucose check; smoking cessation counseling.

Final answer: 1. ASSESSMENT: Late-onset RA (symmetric MCP doughiness/NSAID failure); OA (age/hand predominance); multifactorial arthralgia (depression/immobility). Can't-miss: septic arthritis (prior discitis), GCA/PMR, myeloma (Ca/Cr/anemia). 2. PLAN: Stop Daypro (renal risk), acetaminophen trial, X-ray/CRP only if alters DMARD decision; targeted symptom screen for can't-miss; 4–6 wk f/u.

- Supportive care only for presumed viral URI/bronchiolitis: nasal saline, bulb suction, small frequent feeds; counsel mother on red-flag signs (worsening cough, apnea, poor feeding, fever).

- No antibiotics, bronchodilators, steroids, or further imaging/labs, as these will not alter management in a well-appearing infant with normal CXR and reassuring exam.
- Strict return precautions and follow-up in 24–48 hours (or sooner if symptoms worsen) to reassess respiratory effort and feeding; no routine referral needed unless deterioration occurs.

- Urgent surgical/biliary referral if US confirms choledocholithiasis or symptoms progress; otherwise routine surgical follow-up in 1–2 weeks.

llm_plan:
1. ASSESSMENT:
- Severe constipation (likely opioid-induced or IBS exacerbation in pregnancy): Most likely given 2-week history of no bowel movements, palpable rectal stool, LLQ tenderness without peritonitis, nausea/vomiting, and possible unreported opioid use.
- Acute urinary retention (functional or pain-mediated): Supported by reported 24-hour anuria, suprapubic/LLQ pain, and high urine specific gravity with ketones on UA, without clear infectious markers.
- Opioid intoxication or drug-seeking behavior: Evident from sedation, track marks, inconsistent history, multiple prior positive UDS, and demands for pain medication despite reassuring vital signs.

Can't-miss diagnoses: Pyelonephritis (history of recurrent UTIs, back pain, pregnancy risk); preterm labor or chorioamnionitis (28-week gestation with abdominal pain); appendicitis (LLQ pain with nausea, though atypical location).

2. PLAN:
- Constipation: Administer tap-water enema or oral polyethylene glycol if available; reassess pain and voiding after bowel movement. Avoid routine imaging.
- Urinary retention: Perform one-time straight catheterization to measure residual volume; if >300 mL, leave Foley for 24 hours and reassess. Send catheterized urine for culture only if symptoms persist.
- Drug-related issues: No new opioids; offer non-opioid analgesia (acetaminophen) and monitor for withdrawal. Counsel on substance use with social work referral if available.
- Exclude pyelonephritis: Monitor vital signs and repeat UA after catheterization; start empiric antibiotics (nitrofurantoin) only if fever or CVA tenderness develops.
- Exclude preterm labor: Continuous fetal monitoring for 20–30 minutes if available; if reassuring and no contractions, discharge with close OB follow-up.
- Follow-up: Discharge with bowel regimen (fiber, hydration) and strict return precautions for fever, worsening pain, or decreased fetal movement; schedule next-day OB visit. No broad labs or imaging unless exam changes.

1. ASSESSMENT:
- Completed spontaneous abortion: Most likely given 3 months of daily spotting culminating in passage of tissue-like material 2 weeks ago, now with resolution of bleeding and absence of pain.

- Urine pregnancy test and, if positive, serum quantitative hCG today to confirm ongoing gestation vs. resolving pregnancy.
- Speculum exam with bimanual to assess for active bleeding, retained tissue, or cervical motion tenderness; treat with doxycycline + metronidazole only if signs of infection found.
- CBC and basic metabolic panel (if available) to evaluate anemia and volume status; IV crystalloid bolus if hypotensive or markedly tachycardic after exam.
- No routine imaging or broad labs; pelvic ultrasound only if hCG positive and exam suggests retained products or ectopic (resource-limited).
- Hold tramadol; counsel on safe analgesics; arrange close follow-up in 48 hours or sooner if fever, worsening bleeding, or dizziness develops; provide pregnancy counseling resources given desire to continue gestation.

1. ASSESSMENT:
- Odontogenic infection (periapical abscess or acute apical periodontitis) from fractured tooth #20: focal fracture, alveolar fluctuance/induration, and severe unilateral throbbing pain without systemic signs point directly to localized dental source.
- Irreversible pulpitis from extensive caries/fracture: longstanding decay plus acute fracture explains the nocturnal 9/10 pain that is relieved partially by nerve block.
- Exacerbation of chronic periodontitis: diffuse decay and prior extractions provide the background for acute flare at this site.

Can't-miss diagnoses: (1) cardiac ischemia (referred jaw pain in patient with known CAD and stent); (2) early deep-neck or submandibular-space extension (Ludwig angina precursor).

2. PLAN:
- Dental infection/pulpitis: start narrow-spectrum antibiotic with low cross-reactivity risk given penicillin allergy (e.g., azithromycin 500 mg day 1 then 250 mg daily ×4 days or clindamycin 300 mg TID if tolerated); give NSAID + acetaminophen for ongoing analgesia; urgent outpatient dental referral within 24–48 h for extraction or root canal (source control). No radiographs or labs needed unless swelling spreads.
- Rule out ischemia: obtain ECG now (low-cost, immediately actionable) to exclude active ischemia; if normal and pain is clearly reproduced by dental exam, no further cardiac testing.
- Rule out deep-space infection: serial clinical exams for trismus, floor-of-mouth elevation, or fever; instruct patient to return immediately if these develop. No imaging unless exam changes.
- Medication reconciliation: hold or coordinate antiplatelet management with cardiology before any dental extraction; continue home metoprolol, Synthroid, and potassium.
- Follow-up: dental clinic in 1–2 days; return precautions for worsening swelling, fever, or chest pain; limited prescription of opioids given CAD and addiction risk.

Final answer: see structured ASSESSMENT/PLAN above.

llm_plan:
1. ASSESSMENT:
- Viral bronchiolitis (most likely RSV): 2-month-old with 9-day progressive cough, congestion, post-tussive emesis, hypoxia, retractions, and diffuse crackles in the setting of household smokers and viral prodrome; normal CXR with only bronchial thickening is expected.
- Pertussis: Prolonged paroxysmal cough, post-tussive emesis, incomplete/no immunizations, marked leukocytosis, and afebrile course; household sick contacts increase risk.
- Chlamydial pneumonia: Subacute staccato cough, hypoxia without fever, and monocytosis in a young infant.

Can't-miss diagnoses: Congenital heart disease with left-to-right shunt or mixing lesion (murmur + hypoxia); bacterial pneumonia or sepsis (leukocytosis, hypoxia, and young age).

2. PLAN:
- Admit to pediatrics ward for continuous pulse-oximetry and supplemental oxygen titrated to SpO2 >92%; initiate strict contact precautions and respiratory viral panel (RSV/pertussis PCR) only if cohorting or macrolide decision hinges on result.
- Give azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily × 5 days to cover pertussis and chlamydia while cultures/PCR pending; no other antibiotics unless deterioration.
- Obtain nasopharyngeal pertussis PCR and chest radiograph (already done) to evaluate for secondary bacterial process; withhold echocardiogram unless persistent hypoxia after bronchiolitis treatment or new cardiac findings.
- Encourage small frequent feeds, bulb suctioning, and nasal saline; educate parents on smoke avoidance and return precautions for apnea or worsening distress.
- Follow-up: Daily clinical reassessment while hospitalized; discharge when off oxygen >24 h and feeding well, with close primary-care visit in 48 h.

Final answer: 1. Bronchiolitis (RSV); 2. Pertussis; 3. Chlamydial pneumonia. Can't-miss: CHD, bacterial sepsis. Plan: O2/admit, azithromycin, targeted PCR.

1. ASSESSMENT:
- Physiologic gastroesophageal reflux (normal infant regurgitation): most common cause of occasional non-projectile, curdled, nonbilious spitting in a 2-week-old who is otherwise thriving with normal weight gain, feeding, and exam.
- Normal feeding variant/overfeeding: frequent nursing (q2-3h) with only intermittent small-volume spit-ups and no growth or developmental concerns.
- Cow’s-milk protein sensitivity (mild): possible given curdled appearance, though low likelihood without other signs (rash, blood in stool, poor weight gain).

Can't-miss diagnoses: hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (must exclude if vomiting becomes projectile or weight gain falters); intestinal malrotation/volvulus (exclude if emesis turns bilious).

2. PLAN:
- Reassurance and parental education on normal infant reflux/regurgitation; continue on-demand breastfeeding without restriction; hold upright 20–30 min after feeds and burp frequently; trial smaller, more frequent feeds if volume appears excessive. No medications or formula change indicated at this time.
- Return precautions: seek care for projectile vomiting, bilious emesis, lethargy, poor feeding, or weight loss.
- To exclude pyloric stenosis: clinical monitoring of feeding pattern and weight at next visit (no ultrasound while thriving); same for malrotation (history alone sufficient now).
- Well-child follow-up in 2 weeks for weight check and ongoing surveillance; sooner if symptoms escalate. No labs, imaging, or referrals required.

Final answer: 1. ASSESSMENT: Physiologic GER (normal regurgitation): common, non-projectile curdled spit-ups, thriving 2-wk-old. Normal feeding variant: q2-3h nursing, good gain, no red flags. Mild CMPA: occasional curdled appearance, low likelihood. Can't-miss: Pyloric stenosis (projectile risk); malrotation/volvulus (bilious risk). 2. PLAN: Reassure, upright positioning, frequent burping, smaller feeds prn; return precautions for worsening vomiting/weight loss; clinical f/u 2 wk (no US while thriving); no meds/tests/referrals.

llm_plan:
**ASSESSMENT:**
1. Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (dacryostenosis) – classic history of unilateral epiphora and morning crusting beginning shortly after birth, exacerbated by URIs, with no signs of acute infection.
2. Physiologic epiphora with incomplete canalicular patency – minor anatomic variant that improves spontaneously in most infants by 12–18 months.
3. Mild recurrent conjunctival irritation from tear stasis – secondary low-grade inflammation without bacterial superinfection.

Can't-miss diagnoses: acute dacryocystitis or preseptal cellulitis (would require prompt antibiotics and possible drainage if redness, swelling, or fever develop).

**PLAN:**
- Continue parental lacrimal-sac massage 2–3 times daily; educate on technique and red-flag signs (increasing erythema, purulent discharge, fever).
- No laboratory tests, cultures, or imaging indicated at this time; diagnosis is clinical and management changes only if infection or persistence beyond 18 months occurs.
- If no resolution by 18 months or recurrent infection develops, refer to ophthalmology for possible probing (resource-appropriate timing).

- Check only a single post-void residual by in-and-out catheterization at next visit and serum creatinine once (both directly assess graft-threatening obstruction); no routine UA/culture, PSA, or imaging unless fever, graft tenderness, or rising creatinine develops.
- Reinforce timed voiding and double voiding; return precautions for fever, graft-site pain, or oliguria.
- No new referrals or broad laboratory panels.

Final answer: BPH/obstruction (cystoscopy+), anticholinergic effect (oxybutynin), neurogenic bladder; stop oxybutynin, urology f/u + PVR/Cr only; exclude graft obstruction/UTI by symptoms + targeted Cr/PVR.

llm_plan:
1. ASSESSMENT:
   - Normal pressure hydrocephalus: classic clinical triad (magnetic gait apraxia requiring walker/wheelchair, urge incontinence with pads, and subcortical dementia with MMSE 17/30) plus supportive MRI (ventriculomegaly with frontal horn span 5 cm, effaced corpus callosum, patent aqueduct, pulsation artifact) in the absence of papilledema or mass lesion.
   - Subcortical vascular dementia (Binswanger pattern): extensive confluent T2 white-matter hyperintensities, vascular risk factors (HTN, DM, hyperlipidemia), stepwise or gradual decline, and paratonia without focal weakness.
   - Lewy-body or Parkinson-spectrum disorder: shuffling gait, micrographia, paratonia, family history of PD; early postural instability and autonomic features exceed typical idiopathic PD.

   Can't-miss: chronic subdural hematoma or obstructive mass lesion (MRI already excludes); neurosyphilis or B12 deficiency (reversible mimics of the triad).

2. PLAN:
   - NPH: perform large-volume (30–50 mL) CSF tap test in clinic with pre/post gait and MMSE assessment; if clear improvement, refer for neurosurgical ventriculoperitoneal shunt evaluation. Start outpatient PT for gait safety and fall prevention; no new medications.
   - Vascular dementia: optimize existing regimen (continue lisinopril, metoprolol, Lipitor, metformin, aspirin); add no new labs or imaging unless focal signs emerge.
   - Parkinsonism: do not initiate levodopa trial until after tap test (to avoid confounding gait assessment); monitor for orthostasis.
   - Exclude can't-miss: obtain serum B12 and RPR (single low-cost tests that directly alter management if positive); no additional MRI, EEG, or broad panels.
   - Supportive: refer to social work for home safety evaluation and caregiver support; schedule 4–6 week follow-up to review tap-test result and functional status. No routine carotid imaging, EEG, or specialist referrals at this time.

Final answer: NPH (tap test) > vascular dementia (risk-factor control) > parkinsonism; B12/RPR to exclude reversibles; PT + f/u.

1. ASSESSMENT:
   - Normal pressure hydrocephalus s/p VP shunt (most likely): classic clinical triad with documented improvement in gait (Tinetti) and cognition (MMSE) after programmable shunt placement at level 2.0, consistent with positive response to prior CSF tap test.
   - Residual detrusor instability / BPH-related incontinence: persistent diaper use despite initial modest improvement, on stable Detrol/Flomax, typical in elderly men with comorbid NPH.
   - Chronic small-vessel cerebrovascular disease: extensive white-matter changes on CT plus slow finger-nose testing, contributing to baseline gait and cognitive deficits that only partially reverse after shunting.
   - Can't-miss: shunt malfunction or clinically significant subdural hematoma (tiny extra-axial collection already visible on recent CT; could enlarge on Plavix and cause herniation or acute deterioration).

2. PLAN:
   - NPH post-shunt: continue current Medtronic Strata setting 2.0; no valve adjustment or imaging today because symptoms are improving and patient is headache-free. Counsel daughter on red-flag symptoms (worsening gait, new headache, vomiting) that would prompt urgent return visit.
   - Incontinence: continue Detrol LA + Flomax; no urodynamics or additional urologic referral as symptoms are stable and not limiting daily function.
   - Cerebrovascular disease: continue aspirin alternatives (Plavix), statin, ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker; reinforce vascular risk-factor control (BP already at target).
   - Exclude can't-miss shunt complication: rely on interval history and neurologic exam at next scheduled visit (3 months); obtain non-contrast head CT only if new focal deficit, headache, or gait decline occurs. No routine labs or broad panels.

Final answer: ASSESSMENT: 1. NPH s/p VP shunt (improving); 2. residual detrusor/BPH incontinence; 3. small-vessel CVD. Can't-miss: shunt malfunction/significant SDH. PLAN: continue current shunt setting & meds; red-flag education; CT only if deterioration; f/u 3 mo.

Possible shunt malfunction or clinically significant subdural hematoma
llm_dx_summary: Patient with normal pressure hydrocephalus status post VP shunt placement showing clinical improvement, persistent urinary incontinence likely related to detrusor instability/BPH, chronic small-vessel cerebrovascular disease contributing to baseline deficits, and monitoring for potential shunt complications.

1. ASSESSMENT:
- Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) due to ovulatory dysfunction: most likely given new irregular cycle length, heavy flow with clots, and recent worsening dysmenorrhea in a 19-year-old with reported stress; anovulatory cycles are common in this age group and often exacerbated by psychosocial stress.
- Primary dysmenorrhea: probable contributor to premenstrual cramping and uterine tenderness on exam, without structural findings.
- Menstrual-related migraine: consistent with cyclic worsening headaches temporally linked to menses, absence of focal neurologic signs, and normal fundoscopic exam.

Can't-miss diagnoses: pregnancy (despite reported non-sexual activity, must exclude before any hormonal therapy); coagulopathy (e.g., von Willebrand disease) given objectively heavy bleeding requiring frequent pad changes; intracranial mass or secondary headache cause given new daily migraines.

2. PLAN:
- AUB/ovulatory dysfunction: trial of scheduled NSAIDs (ibuprofen 400 mg TID with menses) for 3 cycles to reduce bleeding and pain; obtain TSH only if no improvement or additional symptoms develop. Counsel on menstrual calendar tracking and stress reduction. No imaging or endometrial biopsy indicated at age 19.
- Primary dysmenorrhea: continue NSAIDs as above; if inadequate, consider cyclic combined oral contraceptive (lowest estrogen dose) for cycle regulation after confirming negative urine pregnancy test today.
- Menstrual migraine: initiate non-pharmacologic measures (sleep hygiene, limit cola/chocolate); add OTC NSAID at headache onset; reserve neuroimaging or neurology referral only for focal deficits, papilledema, or failure of conservative therapy after 3 cycles.
- Can't-miss exclusions: urine hCG today (result will determine safety of any hormonal Rx); inquire about personal/family bleeding history—if positive, pursue CBC and coagulation studies. No routine labs, Pap follow-up per cytology result, return in 3 months or sooner if bleeding worsens or neurologic symptoms appear.

- Exclude can't-miss diagnoses: No new brain MRI indicated (prior study normal, chronic non-progressive course, normal exam apart from tremor/dystonia); monitor for emergence of rest tremor, rigidity, or gait decline at next visit in 6 months; return sooner if new focal deficits or progression.
